mappings.rationale: Requires a topic-specific HR security policy whose mandated contents (screening, roles, acceptable use, training, asset return, NDA, disciplinary reference) are exactly the employment-contract security obligations of 6.2, issued as a policy per 5.1.

Background verification of employees, contractors and third-party users with criteria driven by role, information classification and access to critical areas is verbatim the screening requirement of 6.1.
Terms and conditions of employment stating the security responsibilities of both entity and personnel, read/signed by employees, contractors and third parties, is the direct subject of 6.2.

Three distinct obligations: management ensuring personnel apply security per policy (5.4), an acceptable usage policy signed before access is granted (5.10), and consideration of segregation of duties to prevent misuse of position (5.3).
Formally launched and managed awareness and training programme for employees, contractors and third parties, with effectiveness evaluation and records, is precisely 6.3.
Assessing information security skill and competency gaps and running development programmes is the education/competence limb of 6.3.
Scheduled awareness campaigns for general and targeted user groups, using current risk and incident learnings as content, is the awareness-campaign delivery mechanism 6.3 calls for.
A communicated and enforced disciplinary process for personnel who commit security breaches, with records of breaches and management action, is the whole of 6.4.
Defining who is responsible for security at employment termination or role change, including exit communication and knowledge handover, is the responsibilities-after-termination requirement of 6.5.
Recovery of all organizational assets on termination with signed acknowledgement that no information remains in the leaver's possession is the return-of-assets clause 5.11.
Revoking system, application, information and secure-area access on termination of employment or contract is the removal limb of the access-rights lifecycle in 5.18.
On internal transfer, revoking privileges tied to the old role and reassigning access consistent with the new role on fresh authorization is the modification limb of 5.18.
The asset management policy mandates ownership assignment, accountability and recording of asset properties (5.9) and mandates the four-level AD classification scheme plus retention (5.12).

Defines which roles may access, use and maintain medical devices and requires per-device handling procedures and a risk log — asset ownership/recording (5.9) plus rules for permitted use (5.10); ISO 27002 has no medical-device-specific clause, so the fit is partial.
Identifying, recording and periodically updating all information assets in an inventory that captures inter-asset dependencies is exactly the inventory requirement of 5.9.
Assigning a named owner per asset who defines controls, reviews their adequacy and authorizes access is the asset-ownership limb explicitly stated in 5.9.
Establishing, communicating and obtaining signed acknowledgement of rules for acceptable use of information assets is the direct subject of 5.10.

BYOD risk addressed through role-based usage agreements and technical controls before personal devices may access or store PHI is the personally-owned-device provision of 8.1, governed by acceptable-use rules (5.10).
Classifying every information asset into the Public/Restricted/Confidential/Secret scheme is the classification requirement of 5.12.

Requiring the value of the information and the entity's tolerance of financial impact to drive how restrictive the classification is, is the value-and-impact criterion 5.12 says classification must be based on.
Determining classification from the level of protection an asset essentially needs is a criterion for the 5.12 classification decision, though ADHICS states it as a standalone one-line rule.
Reassessing and changing classification when information value, environment or protection level changes is the periodic-review limb of 5.12.
Interpreting another organization's classification scheme on received information maps to 5.12's requirement to align schemes across organizations and to 5.13's handling of labels applied by others.
Setting criteria for automated classification and deploying tooling to apply the scheme is an implementation method for 5.12, not a separate ISO control.
Labelling information assets in physical and digital form consistently with the classification scheme is precisely 5.13.

Handling procedures specifying security requirements for access, processing, storage, sharing and printing per classification are the classification-driven handling rules folded into 5.10, keyed off the labels of 5.13.
Ensuring the handling procedures are actually adopted and applied is an enforcement/compliance-verification obligation (5.36) over the asset-handling rules of 5.10.
Removable media management procedures covering setup, distribution, utilization, disposal and protection during movement is the storage-media lifecycle clause 7.10.
Requiring management authorization and formal risk acceptance before removable media may be used is the authorization limb of 7.10.

Documented management procedures per category of medical device are operating procedures (5.37) for a class of inventoried asset (5.9); ISO has no clinical-equipment clause so this is a structural rather than substantive match.
Allocating medical-device access and privileges only to defined roles holding required qualifications is role-based access provisioning under 5.15 and privilege allocation under 5.18.
Mandates encryption of patient information stored on medical devices and of communications between them (8.24), plus moving copies of valuable health data to secure storage against loss (8.13).
Requiring wired connectivity for medical devices and avoiding wireless is a network-security design constraint on how devices are connected, covered generically by 8.20.
Whitelisting permitted removable media devices is a storage-media control (7.10), with mandated content encryption falling under 8.24.
Authorizing and recording the removal, movement and transfer of equipment, devices and media off site is the off-premises asset protection of 7.9 and the media-movement limb of 7.10.
Disposing of information assets once no longer required by the entity, regulation or legal hold is information deletion (8.10) and, where the asset is equipment, secure disposal (7.14).
Requiring a control process that guarantees destroyed data cannot be recovered is the irreversible-deletion requirement of 8.10.
Destroying both digital and physical media once no longer required is the media-disposal limb of 7.10 and the secure-disposal requirement of 7.14.
Procedures for secure disposal or re-use of media, equipment and systems ensuring classified data and licensed software are removed beyond recovery first is verbatim 7.14.
Verifying that retention obligations for the contained data are satisfied before disposal is a records-retention check (5.33) gating the deletion action (8.10).
Requiring management authorization before any disposal is the approval step within the secure disposal process of 7.14.

Maintaining disposal records naming owner, media type, classification, method, authorizer and removal evidence is the documented-disposal-record expectation under 7.14 for storage media handled per 7.10.

A topic-specific physical and environmental security policy (5.1) whose stated substance is protection from internal/external and environmental threats including hazardous and combustible material storage (7.5).
Establishing supporting procedures and guidelines to implement the physical security policy is the documented-operating-procedures requirement of 5.37.

Requires the policy to address placement and physical access of equipment and medical devices (7.8) and the risk of data loss during maintenance, decommissioning and authorized off-site activity (7.13).
Defining security perimeters around facilities based on the information and systems contained within, and identifying secure areas, is the direct subject of 7.1.
Allocating secure private areas in which authorized staff may discuss personal health information is the securing-of-rooms-and-facilities requirement of 7.3 applied to conversation privacy.
Authorized-personnel lists, authentication at entry, access records, visible badges, door locking/alarms and escorting of contractors are the physical entry controls of 7.2.
Requires nominated owners to review secure-area access logs and surveillance footage quarterly (7.4) and to reconcile the authorized-user and physical key inventories (7.2).
Equipping offices and meeting rooms with physical security, demarcating public from key work areas and avoiding signage that reveals activities is exactly 7.3.
Designing physical protection against natural disasters, environmental threats, external attack and accidents, including protecting fall-back equipment and backup media, is 7.5.
Requires physical and environmental countermeasures to remain aligned with risk-assessment outcomes (7.5) and with regulatory mandates, which is a compliance-verification duty under 5.36.
Guidelines for working in secure areas, supervision of activities there and control of mobile and recording devices brought in is verbatim 7.6.
Ensuring everyone entering secure areas knows and accepts the rules (7.6) is delivered through staff education, including not discussing PHI in public areas (6.3).
Segregated delivery and loading areas with entry/exit controls and inspection and registration of incoming material is the delivery-and-loading-area provision explicitly inside 7.2.
Siting equipment and medical devices so they are protected from unauthorized access and environmental risk conditions is the whole of 7.8.
Protecting equipment from disruption caused by supporting-utility failure and ensuring uninterrupted power to processing systems is verbatim 7.11.
Maintaining equipment per supplier recommendations on a documented schedule with up-to-date maintenance records is the equipment-maintenance clause 7.13.
Protecting power, telecommunication and data cabling against tampering and segregating power from data cabling to avoid interference is verbatim 7.12.
Applying security measures and chain-of-custody logging to equipment, medical devices and processing systems while off-site is the off-premises asset clause 7.9.
Defining user responsibilities and controls for equipment left unattended is the unattended-equipment requirement that ISO 27002:2022 folded into the clear desk and clear screen clause 7.7.
An enforced clear desk and clear screen policy covering paper, removable media and processing systems, acknowledged by all staff, is the direct subject of 7.7.
An access control policy establishing need-to-know and role-based access criteria across information, applications, technology and medical devices is the topic-specific access control clause 5.15.

Formal user registration/de-registration with a unique account per individual and no shared or group accounts is identity management (5.16); revocation at exit and revalidation at role change is 5.18.
Restricting allocation of administrative privileges, separating privileged accounts from day-to-day accounts and barring normal accounts from service or privileged use is verbatim 8.2.
Secure allocation, use and management of passwords — changing defaults, hashed storage, out-of-band initial delivery, complexity rules — is the authentication-information clause 5.17.
Authenticating access to mobile and portable devices and enforcing password/encryption on them is 8.1; the same requirement applied to removable media carrying confidential data is 7.10.
Controlling authentication and authorization for equipment and facilities at teleworking sites, including telemedicine delivery, is the remote-working clause 6.7.
At-least-annual review of granted user access and privileges by defined reviewers, with an up-to-date inventory of access, is the periodic-review limb of 5.18.
Granting access to networks and network services only for the specific need the user is authorized for is the access-control principle of 5.15 applied to the network layer governed by 8.20.
Requiring remote logins over secure channels with multifactor authentication is the secure-authentication clause 8.5 applied to the remote-access scenario of 6.7.
Automated detection of unauthorized equipment on the network is a monitoring activity (8.16) reconciled against the recorded asset inventory (5.9).
Whitelisting diagnostic ports and services and disabling those not required is configuration hardening (8.9); restricting and logging use of troubleshooting and diagnostic utilities is 8.18.

Restricting user connection to shared versus isolated networks per the access control policy is the network-connection control that ISO 27002:2022 folded into networks security (8.20) and network segregation (8.22).

Routing rules enforcing source/destination and port checks with anti-manipulation protection so traffic follows controlled paths is the routing-control requirement absorbed into 8.20, and its zoning effect into 8.22.
Secure wireless configuration and authorization (8.20), isolation of guest and public wireless from the internal network (8.22) and strong cryptographic authentication of wireless connections (8.24).
Secure log-on and log-off procedures with authenticated access, inactivity locking, idle session timeout and automatic session termination is verbatim the secure-authentication clause 8.5.
Issuing each user a unique identifier is the core of identity management (5.16); requiring all user activity to be logged against that identifier is 8.15.
Restricting, authorizing, inventorying and monitoring the use of utility programs capable of overriding system and application controls is verbatim 8.18.

Restricting access to information and application system functions on need-to-know with role-based enforcement, explicitly excluding ancillary staff from healthcare data, is the information-access-restriction clause 8.3.
Isolating sensitive systems in a dedicated environment is the sensitive-system-isolation requirement that ISO 27002:2022 absorbed into segregation of networks (8.22).

Preventing accidental or deliberate exposure of non-public information to the public domain, with periodic validation that none has leaked, is a leakage-prevention control (8.12) enforcing the access restriction of 8.3.

An operations management policy (5.1) whose enumerated substance — SoD, configuration, change control, baselines, standard operating procedures, capacity, acceptance, malware — is the documented-operating-procedures regime of 5.37.
Developing and enforcing baseline and recommended secure configuration settings for IT products, applications and medical devices is verbatim configuration management (8.9).
Documenting, disseminating and keeping current the operating procedures for all support and maintenance activities, including up-to-date system diagrams, is the direct subject of 5.37.
A Change Advisory Board and a formal change process covering recording, testing, impact assessment, approval, communication, rollback and post-implementation review is verbatim 8.32.
Requiring movement of systems from development or project state into production to pass through the authorization and change process is 8.32 governing the environment boundary of 8.31.
Identifying conflicting roles, assigning them to different individuals and applying compensating controls where that is impossible is verbatim segregation of duties (5.3).
Separating development, test, staging and operational environments with controlled transfer between them and a bar on using live data in test is verbatim 8.31.
Documenting current and future capacity needs, monitoring and measuring capacity, and setting thresholds with an escalation matrix is verbatim capacity management (8.6).
Acceptance criteria for new systems, changes, upgrades and releases with documented test cases and results required before production use is the acceptance-testing clause 8.29.
Anti-malware protection across networks, servers, workstations and mobile devices with current signatures, real-time protection, scheduled scans and removable-media scanning is verbatim 8.7.
Gateway-level malware detection for web and email traffic is 8.7; technology that blocks access to malicious or prohibited-category websites is web filtering (8.23).
Backup process identifying critical data, owners, RPO/RTO, frequency and methods, with restoration testing, is verbatim the information backup clause 8.13.
Archival criteria and retention periods set by law and regulation with preservation of archived data is records protection (5.33); destroying data past its retention timeline is 8.10.
Monitoring procedures defining what is monitored (system use, changes, unauthorized activity, exceptions, access), at what frequency and by what method is verbatim monitoring activities (8.16).
Enabling audit logs of administrator, operator and user activity, exceptions and security events, with defined minimum log content, review frequency and retention, is verbatim 8.15.

Centralized log preservation with access control, retention and administration by staff independent of system operations is the log-protection limb of 8.15; the required use cases and dashboards are 8.16.
Synchronizing all information system clocks (including medical devices) to an agreed time source with a standardized format and regular verification is verbatim 8.17.

Formal patching procedure with criteria for standard, urgent and critical patches, prompt application of critical security patches and pilot testing before mass deployment is the remediation limb of 8.8.
Monitoring processing systems for leakage opportunities and implementing DLP measures is verbatim the data leakage prevention clause 8.12.
Scheduled penetration testing, vulnerability assessment and web security assessment across systems, networks and applications is the identification limb of technical vulnerability management (8.8).

Restricting what system and network information assessors may hold and requiring erasure of assessment outputs from third-party assets after engagement protects systems during audit testing (8.34) and must be written into the assessor agreement (5.20).

A communications policy (5.1) whose substance is protection of information in transit and in exchange, exchange agreements, electronic and physical transfer modes — the information transfer clause 5.14.
Formal information exchange and transfer procedures with control measures based on classification and value, plus technical standards for packaging health information, is verbatim 5.14.
Protecting critical information in transit is 5.14; the specified mechanism — encrypt before transfer and deliver the key over a different channel — is the cryptography clause 8.24.

Protecting information exchanged within the entity, between entities and across sharing communities, including interoperability standards for system-to-system transfer, is the information transfer clause 5.14.

Formal transfer agreements with external parties setting roles, responsibilities and security requirements before exchange begins is the transfer-agreement limb of 5.14; the required non-disclosure terms are 6.6.

Ensuring external parties are aware of and have effectively implemented the agreed security requirements is the agreement-content and assurance obligation of 5.20 applied to the transfer arrangements of 5.14.

Protecting classified physical media in transit against disclosure, loss and modification, with tracking and trusted couriers, is the media-in-transit provision of 7.10 within the transfer regime of 5.14.
Categorising electronic messaging channels, setting per-channel controls and requiring messages go only to authorized recipients is the electronic-messaging limb of information transfer (5.14).

Identifying interconnection and integration points between business information systems and protecting the information crossing them is the business-information-system transfer provision absorbed into 5.14.

Protecting e-commerce services traversing public networks against fraud, contract dispute and unauthorized disclosure or modification is the transactional-application security requirement enumerated in 8.26.
Protecting online transactions against incomplete transmission, misrouting, message alteration, disclosure and replay or duplication is the transactional-services provision stated in 8.26.

Sanitising and approving information before publication and keeping publicly accessible systems available and unmodified is the publicly-available-application provision of 8.26, backstopped by leakage prevention (8.12).

Inventorying information-sharing platforms and defining security requirements for connecting to or releasing information into them is a network-service security requirement (8.21) governing an information transfer arrangement (5.14).

Prohibiting cloud storage or processing of health information and requiring disconnection of cloud-integrated systems is a cloud-service security decision (5.23); the bar on transmitting health data outside the UAE is a statutory data-residency obligation under 5.31, which ISO states generically without any geographic constraint.

Strictly controlling access to national health information exchange platforms with periodic revalidation of who needs it is the access-control policy of 5.15 enforced through the access-rights review of 5.18.
Managing, documenting and protecting all networks and supporting infrastructure, with current diagrams and controls chosen against identified network threats, is verbatim networks security (8.20).
Identifying security requirements, service levels and management requirements for each network service and including them in network service agreements is verbatim 8.21.
Segregating physical, logical and wireless networks into security zones by criticality with per-zone requirements and periodic adequacy review is verbatim segregation of networks (8.22).

Site surveys to contain stray signal, trusted-device-only access and guest isolation are wireless network security under 8.20; the mandated strong authentication and cryptographic methods on access points are 8.24.

A health information protection policy (5.1) setting access criteria, data ownership, sharing rules, confidentiality obligations and legal sanctions for patient data is the privacy and PII protection clause 5.34.

Protecting healthcare information in the entity's custody through enforced access criteria and stricter clear-desk practice in PHI-handling areas is 5.34; the mandatory pre-access orientation on PHI protection and sanctions is 6.3.

A third party security policy framing secure management of supplier services, security objectives and supplier briefing to reduce third-party risk is verbatim information security in supplier relationships (5.19).
Embedding per-service security requirements, minimum baselines and service levels into third-party service agreements is verbatim addressing information security within supplier agreements (5.20).
Monitoring supplier compliance with agreed security requirements and having qualified staff review supplier reports and records is the monitoring and review limb of 5.22.
Managing changes to third-party service provisions through a formal process written into the agreement is the change-management limb of 5.22.

A policy establishing secure development and maintenance practices and the selection of the development model across internal and external stakeholders is the secure development life cycle clause 8.25.
Analysing, specifying and approving security requirements for new systems and enhancements, addressing identified risk elements, is verbatim application security requirements (8.26).

Requiring developers to receive baseline and security-feature-specific training before joining development work is the developer-competence expectation of secure coding (8.28), delivered through the training regime of 6.3.

Defining validation rules for application input and dropping data identified as incorrect is the input-validation requirement ISO 27002:2022 absorbed into application security requirements (8.26) and secure coding practice (8.28).
Embedding validation checks that detect corruption of information from processing errors or deliberate acts is the internal-processing control ISO 27002:2022 merged into 8.26 and 8.28.
Ensuring authenticity and integrity of messages exchanged between applications is normally delivered by the cryptographic mechanisms of 8.24, specified as an application requirement under 8.26.
Defining rules and parameters to validate application output as correct and appropriate is the output-validation control ISO 27002:2022 folded into 8.26 and 8.28.

Requiring distributed and mobile applications to tolerate communication failure and handle duplicate or out-of-sequence responses is a resilience design requirement — related to the application requirements of 8.26 and the engineering principles of 8.27, but ISO has no direct equivalent.
Key generation, revocation, recovery, strength standards, storage and protection of secret and private keys is the key-management limb explicitly inside 8.24.
Restricting software installation on operational systems to authorized staff, retaining previous versions and routing installs through change approval is verbatim 8.19.
Using sample datasets rather than production data, authorizing and recording any use of real data, barring PII as test data and erasing it afterwards is verbatim test information (8.33).
Restricting access to program source code strictly on need and per the access control policy is verbatim access to source code (8.4).

Supervising outsourced software development and contractually binding the developer to secure coding policy, quality assurance and entity/regulatory requirements is verbatim outsourced development (8.30).

A strategy against supply chain threats to systems and medical devices — acquisition policy, limits on sharing architecture with suppliers, acceptance criteria, right-to-audit clauses — is verbatim ICT supply chain security (5.21).
A defined evaluation process for suppliers before contracting is the supplier-selection limb of 5.19; periodic review of supplier compliance with agreement terms is 5.22.

Limiting what is shared with suppliers, sharing only over secure channels and diversifying suppliers for critical products to deny adversaries a supply-chain foothold are supply chain risk measures under 5.21.
Evaluating risk to systems, medical devices and support operations from the supply chain (5.21) and agreeing the resulting control measures in supplier contracts (5.20).

Verifying that delivered systems, components and medical devices are genuine and that software has not been altered to insert back doors or covert channels is the component-authenticity and anti-tamper provision of 5.21.
Documenting supply chain elements and their interdependencies and addressing identified issues is 5.21; the regular assessments and audits of those elements are the supplier-service review of 5.22.
Contingency plans, stockpiled spares and multiple suppliers for critical components exist to keep ICT available through disruption (5.30) and are a supply-chain continuity measure under 5.21.
An incident management policy establishing roles, responsibilities and a sustainable process for identifying and resolving incidents is verbatim incident management planning and preparation (5.24).
Tested procedures for handling incidents before, during and after occurrence with stakeholder and authority communication planned is the response clause 5.26, prepared under 5.24.

Standing up a CSIRT with defined authority, competent named role-holders, communication protocols and funding is the preparation clause 5.24; the required coordination with the Abu Dhabi health sector regulator is contact with authorities (5.5).
Assessing and classifying security incidents against a defined severity scheme with per-class handling workflows is verbatim assessment and decision on information security events (5.25).
Testing incident response capability against expected outcomes and closing identified gaps is the plan-exercise expectation within incident management preparation (5.24).
Procedures for identifying, collecting and preserving incident evidence addressing chain of custody, safety, personnel competency and documentation is verbatim collection of evidence (5.28).
Institutionalising lessons learned from past incidents into a knowledge base to reduce recurrence is verbatim learning from information security incidents (5.27).

Obtaining cybersecurity information from multiple sources and contextualising it to the entity's systems and processes is threat intelligence (5.7); participation in the information sharing community is contact with special interest groups (5.6).
A formal reporting channel with designated points of contact and staff and third-party awareness of the duty to report security events is verbatim information security event reporting (6.8).
Reporting observed or suspected security weaknesses through a formal channel and prohibiting users from exploiting them is the weakness-reporting limb of 6.8.

A continuity planning policy for scenarios threatening availability of systems supporting critical services sets management expectations for maintaining security during disruption (5.29) and ICT continuity readiness (5.30).

Developing ICT continuity plans that identify the systems supporting critical services, assign roles and align with organizational BC/DR planning is verbatim ICT readiness for business continuity (5.30).
Ensuring the capabilities the continuity plans depend on are actually established and available at activation is the implementation limb of 5.30.
Scheduled testing of ICT continuity plans for adequacy and resource readiness, documenting outcomes and updating plans after change or lessons learned, is the test-and-maintain limb of 5.30.
